screens.title: Sending Transactions and Modifying Contract State
screens.subtitle: How transactions change blockchain state, cost gas, and must be signed and monitored.

narration.text: In this chapter we move from reading data to changing it. You will learn what a transaction is, why gas is required, and how to send transactions from a frontend using both Web3. js and Ethers. js. We’ll cover required parameters like from, to, value, gas limit, gas price and the encoded data payload, and you’ll see concrete examples of updating a contract message and depositing Ether. You will practice signing transactions with a connected account or a wallet, observe transaction lifecycles from pending to mined, and learn how to handle common failures like reverts and insufficient funds. This matters because state changes are the core of any DApp: minting tokens, moving funds, or changing ownership all require reliable transaction handling. By the end you’ll be able to send a state-changing call, wait for confirmations, and surface informative errors to users. Consider a simple counter contract: the steps we learn here are exactly what increments and stores that count on-chain. Are you ready to see how a single signed message becomes an immutable state change?

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Transactions are signed messages that change contract state and consume gas; frontends must create, sign, send, and monitor them carefully.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These learning objectives map directly to practical skills you need when building DApps that change blockchain state. First, you’ll understand the full lifecycle of a transaction: how signing, gas, and mining work together to make a state change permanent. Second, you’ll be able to call state-modifying functions from the frontend using both Web3. js and Ethers. js, including passing Ether when a function is payable. Third, you will implement signing and sending transactions with a connected account or a signer object, and learn safe handling to avoid exposing private keys. Finally, you’ll learn to monitor transactions, read receipts, and surface failures such as reverts or insufficient funds to users. Each objective includes a short practice cue so you can test the skill. These goals ensure you move beyond reading blockchain state into reliably and safely modifying it in real applications.

screens.title: What is a Transaction?
screens.subtitle: Definition, lifecycle, and why gas is required

narration.text: A transaction is a cryptographically signed message that requests a change to the Ethereum state. It can call a contract function that writes data, transfer Ether, or trigger events. Transactions are not instant — they are broadcast, collected by miners or validators, included in a block, and then become part of the chain. That entire work costs gas, a unit that measures computation and storage used. You pay for gas with Ether; the network consumes the fee regardless of whether a transaction succeeds or reverts. A concrete example: calling a contract’s updateMessage will be packaged into a transaction, signed by your account, and included in a block. If the function executes successfully, the message state updates; if it reverts due to a require failing, the state does not change but you still pay for gas used up to the revert point. A common misconception is that a failed transaction costs nothing — in truth, you still pay for the computation performed. Key takeaway: treat transactions as paid operations that require proper signing, sufficient gas, and monitoring for success. How will you surface to users that a transaction is pending and then confirmed?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A transaction is a signed request to change state that consumes gas and is recorded when mined.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › What is a Transaction?
Transaction lifecycle
  1. Construct and sign a transaction with the sender's private key or injected signer.
  2. Broadcast the signed message to the network; it enters the mempool.
  3. A miner/validator includes the tx in a block and executes it, consuming gas.
  4. When the block is mined, a transaction receipt is produced and stored on-chain.
Key Takeaway

A transaction always costs gas and must be awaited until a receipt confirms the state change.

Concrete example
// Example: updateMessage will be sent as a transaction
// Sign the tx, network executes it, and a receipt is returned after mining.
Common misconception: a failed transaction doesn't cost gas. In reality, any computation before the revert consumes gas and is charged. Always estimate gas and add a buffer.
Why it matters
Understanding lifecycle helps you present accurate UX and avoid assumptions that a pending tx is instantaneous.

screens.title: Transaction Parameters Explained
screens.subtitle: from, to, value, gasLimit, gasPrice, and data

narration.text: When you build or send a transaction you must supply several parameters that determine who pays, where value flows, and how much work is allowed. The from address is the account initiating the transaction and must have enough Ether for fees and any value transferred. The to address is either the recipient of Ether or the contract address when calling a contract method. Value is the amount of Ether sent with the call and is meaningful only for payable functions or direct transfers; remember to convert Ether to Wei before sending. Gas limit is the maximum units of gas the transaction can consume; if the execution needs more, the tx will revert and you still pay for the gas consumed. Gas price is the amount you pay per gas unit and influences inclusion speed. The data field contains the encoded function selector and arguments for contract interactions. Concrete example: calling deposit with a value of 0.05 Ether requires setting value to the Wei equivalent and a sensible gasLimit for the call. A common mistake is supplying value to a non-payable function, which will cause an on-chain revert. As you send transactions, always validate the from balance, estimate gas and convert value to Wei, and then submit the signed call.

keyIdea.title: Parameter checklist
keyIdea.text: Supply from, to, correct value in Wei, an estimated gasLimit, and optionally gasPrice to control inclusion.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Transaction Parameters
Parameter reference
  • from: signer address that pays fees and signs the tx.
  • to: recipient or contract address.
  • value: Ether to transfer, in Wei for transmission.
  • gasLimit: maximum gas units allowed for execution.
  • gasPrice: Wei per gas unit to influence miners/validators.
  • data: ABI-encoded function call and parameters.
Tip: always ensure from has balance >= gasLimit * gasPrice + value.
Concrete scenario
You want to call deposit on a contract and send 0.05 Ether. Convert 0.05 Ether to Wei, set the value field to that Wei amount, and provide a gasLimit sufficient for the function. If deposit is payable, it will accept Ether; if it's not, the transaction reverts.
Common mistake
Sending value to a non-payable function causes a revert. Validate function mutability before adding value.
Key Takeaway

Double-check value units and gas math before sending a transaction to avoid costly mistakes.

screens.title: Sending Transactions with Web3.js
screens.subtitle: Using .send(), specifying from, gas, and value

narration.text: Web3. js sends state-changing calls using the send method on a contract method. After you instantiate a contract with its ABI and address, you call contract. methods. myFunction(args). send and supply an options object that includes from, value and gas. The send call returns a Promise that resolves with a transaction receipt once the transaction is mined. A practical example from the source is calling updateMessage with. send({ from: senderAccount, gas: 300000 }), then reading the updated value with a subsequent call. For Ether transfers to payable functions, convert Ether to Wei using the utility conversion and pass value in Wei. Error handling is essential: place the send call inside a try... catch so you can capture reverts and insufficient funds errors, and present a clear message to the user. A common misconception is to assume. send returns immediately with finality; in truth you must await the Promise and then inspect the receipt to confirm the state change. In local testing with Ganache, you can watch transaction hashes and confirm balances with getBalance after receipts arrive. Practice: use accounts[0] from Ganache, call deposit with value in Wei, await the receipt, then check the contract balance.

keyIdea.title: Web3.js pattern
keyIdea.text: .send() submits a signed transaction and resolves with a receipt once mined; always await and handle errors.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Web3.js: .send()
Code (illustrative)
// Instantiate contract with ABI and address
const myMutable = new web3.eth.Contract(ABI, ADDRESS);
const newMessage = "Hello from Cohortia!";
try {
  const receipt = await myMutable.methods.updateMessage(newMessage).send({
    from: sender, gas: 300000
  });
  // receipt contains transactionHash, gasUsed, events
} catch (error) {
  // handle revert or insufficient funds
}

// Deposit Ether (convert to Wei first)
const amountWei = web3.utils.toWei('0.05', 'ether');
await myMutable.methods.deposit().send({ from: sender, value: amountWei, gas: 100000 });
Highlights
  • Use .send and await the Promise for the receipt.
  • Provide a from address and any value in Wei.
  • Wrap calls in try...catch to handle reverts or funding errors.
Pro tip
Test transactions on Ganache to inspect receipts and event logs locally before production.
Key Takeaway

With Web3.js, .send handles broadcasting and returns the mined receipt; always await and validate it.

screens.title: Sending Transactions with Ethers.js and Signer
screens.subtitle: Connect a Signer, call functions, and use tx.wait()

narration.text: Ethers. js centers around the concept of a Signer, which represents an account capable of signing transactions. When you create a Contract instance connected to a Signer or Wallet, calling a state-changing function returns a transaction object rather than a final receipt. You typically call the method, receive a transaction response with a hash, and then call wait on that response to get the receipt after mining. For example, connecting a Wallet with a private key to a JsonRpcProvider and then calling updateMessage returns a tx you can await with tx. wait(). That pattern separates sending from confirmation, letting you present the transaction hash immediately and then confirm or fail after wait resolves. For payable calls, pass value and gasLimit options in the last argument. A common misconception is that the tx response proves finality; instead, use tx. wait to ensure inclusion. Also avoid hardcoding private keys in production; injected providers like browser wallets give you a Signer without exposing keys. Practically, use try... catch around both the send and the wait calls to capture errors raised at either step.

keyIdea.title: Ethers pattern
keyIdea.text: Use a Signer-bound contract, call the function to get a transaction response, then await tx.wait() for the receipt.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Ethers.js & Signer
Essential flow
Create a provider, build or obtain a Signer, and attach it to a Contract. Call the function, receive a tx response, then await tx.wait() to get the receipt and confirm the state change.
// Connect wallet to provider
const wallet = new ethers.Wallet(privateKey, provider);
const contract = new ethers.Contract(ADDRESS, ABI, wallet);
const tx = await contract.updateMessage('Hello', { gasLimit: 300000 });
console.log('Tx hash:', tx.hash);
const receipt = await tx.wait(); // confirmed here
Notes
  • tx.hash is available immediately; it does not equal confirmation.
  • Use tx.wait to ensure the transaction was included.
  • Wrap sending and waiting in try...catch for robust error handling.
Warning
Do not hardcode private keys in production. Use an injected provider so the user signs locally.
Key Takeaway

Ethers splits send and confirmation into tx response and wait; use both for clear UX.

screens.title: Estimating Gas and Setting a Safe Gas Limit
screens.subtitle: Use estimateGas, add a buffer, and avoid out-of-gas failures

narration.text: Estimating gas is a practical defense against out-of-gas reverts. Both Web3. js and Ethers. js expose estimate tools: call contract. methods. myFunction(). estimateGas in Web3 or myContract. estimateGas. myFunction in Ethers to receive an estimate of gas units needed. Use the estimate as a baseline and add a small percentage buffer to account for variable execution paths or future code changes. For example, if estimateGas returns 80,000, supplying a gasLimit of 100,000 gives room for unexpected branching. Remember that if a transaction reaches its gasLimit, it reverts and you still pay for the gas consumed. A common error is setting gas limits too low to save cost; this can cost more due to wasted fees on reverted transactions. Also ensure your account balance covers gasLimit * gasPrice plus any value you intend to send. In practice, automate gas estimation, display an estimated fee to the user, and only allow submission when the payer has sufficient funds. Finally, on test networks like Ganache, inspect gasUsed in the receipt to calibrate future estimates for similar operations. Estimating Gas and Setting a Safe Gas Limit means estimate gas programmatically, add a buffer, and ensure balance covers gas cost plus value to prevent failures.. In practical terms, use estimategas, add a buffer, and avoid out-of-gas failures. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Gas safety
keyIdea.text: Estimate gas programmatically, add a buffer, and ensure balance covers gas cost plus value to prevent failures.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Estimate Gas
Estimate pattern
Call the RPC estimate methods to get a suggested gas amount, then add a buffer. Example: estimated 80,000 → submit 100,000.
Web3.js: methods.myFunction().estimateGas({ from, value })
Ethers.js: myContract.estimateGas.myFunction(args)
Key Takeaway

Never guess gas: estimate programmatically and add a margin to avoid wasted reverts.

Practical checklist
  • Estimate gas for the exact call and parameters.
  • Add a small buffer to the estimate to tolerate variability.
  • Verify the sender’s balance covers gasLimit * gasPrice + value.
  • Log gasUsed from receipts to refine future estimates.
Common mistake
Setting gas too low to save cost often results in reverts and wasted fees; estimate instead of guessing.

screens.title: Common Transaction Errors and How to Handle Them
screens.subtitle: Reverts, insufficient funds, and non-payable value sends

narration.text: When sending transactions you will encounter a small set of recurrent errors. First, insufficient funds happens when the sender does not have enough Ether to cover the fee plus any transferred value. The frontend should calculate gasLimit * gasPrice + value before submitting and block the transaction with a clear message. Second, a transaction can revert on-chain because a require() statement failed or some invariant was not met. In these cases the receipt still shows gasUsed and the state is unchanged. To surface helpful feedback, wrap sending and waiting in try... catch and examine the error reason or data payload where available; many environments include a revert reason. Third, sending value to a non-payable function will cause an immediate revert. Validate contract function mutability before adding value. Finally, private-key exposure is a security error: never hardcode keys in production. Use injected providers so the user’s wallet signs locally. The common misconception is that all errors are identical; distinguish between client-side checks (balance) and on-chain failures (reverts) and present targeted guidance to the user. For practice, intentionally trigger the require-based revert in a Counter decrement when count equals zero and observe how the error propagates to your try... catch.

keyIdea.title: Error handling
keyIdea.text: Differentiate insufficient funds, reverts, and non-payable value sends; use try...catch and clear user messages.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Common Errors
Frequent failures
  • Insufficient funds: check pre-flight balance against total cost.
  • Revert on-chain: validate function preconditions and catch revert reasons.
  • Non-payable value: only attach value to payable functions.
  • Out of gas: estimate and add a buffer.
Handling pattern
  1. Perform client-side checks for balance and input validity.
  2. Call the tx inside try...catch to capture RPC or revert errors.
  3. Inspect error.reason or error.data when available to produce a friendly message.
Practice challenge
Trigger the Counter decrement revert and see how your catch block surfaces the revert message to the user.
Key Takeaway

Different errors require different UX responses: detect client-side issues early and parse on-chain revert details when possible.

screens.title: Monitoring Transaction Status and Reading Receipts
screens.subtitle: From pending to mined: transaction hash, confirmations, and receipt fields

narration.text: After sending a transaction you usually get a transaction response or a promise that resolves to a receipt when mined. The immediate response often contains the transaction hash so you can show the user that the network has accepted the submission. However, inclusion is confirmed only after mining; use tx. wait() in Ethers or await the Promise from Web3. js. send() to receive the receipt. A receipt includes gasUsed, blockNumber, and logs of emitted events — these fields allow you to verify what changed and to trigger UI updates. Many frontends also show confirmations: a transaction may be included in a block but you may wait for additional confirmations for extra finality. In local testing with Ganache, waiting for a single confirmation is usually sufficient. For production, consider the required confirmations for your risk model. A common misconception is to treat a transaction hash as proof of completion; instead, rely on the mined receipt. Present a progressive UI: pending status with the hash, then confirmed with receipt details, and finally application state updated after reading events or querying contract state. This workflow improves user trust and reduces accidental double submissions.

keyIdea.title: Monitoring pattern
keyIdea.text: Display tx hash immediately, then await a mined receipt to confirm and extract gasUsed, blockNumber and events.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Monitoring & Receipts
Progressive status UI
  1. Show tx hash immediately after send so user has reference.
  2. Await receipt via tx.wait() or .send() Promise to confirm inclusion.
  3. Extract gasUsed, blockNumber and logs to verify effects and update state.
  4. Optionally wait for extra confirmations depending on risk tolerance.
Receipt example fields
  • transactionHash: identifier for the tx.
  • gasUsed: actual gas consumed during execution.
  • blockNumber: the block that included the tx.
  • logs: emitted events to trigger UI changes.
Why it matters
Using the receipt to confirm state avoids premature assumptions and improves user trust.

screens.title: Counter Contract Exercise (Web3.js and Ethers.js)
screens.subtitle: Deploy Counter.sol and use sendTx.js to increment and observe reverts

narration.text: The hands-on exercise solidifies the patterns we’ve covered. Deploy the provided Counter contract to Ganache, record its address and ABI, then create a script that interacts with it via both Web3. js and Ethers. js. Using Web3. js, call increment and decrement with. send and await their receipts; observe the count change with a follow-up call to count(). For Ethers. js, create a Wallet signer using your test private key and call increment, await tx. wait(), and then read count from the contract bound to the provider. Intentionally trigger a revert by calling decrement when the counter is zero to see how try... catch captures the failure — this illustrates that the transaction reverts on-chain and you still pay gas. Observe transaction hashes and receipts for both frameworks and inspect gasUsed to learn appropriate gasLimit settings. The activity mirrors the sample sendTx. js: run it, watch the console logs for transaction hashes and receipts, and use the receipts to assert that the contract’s state changed only when the transaction succeeded. This exercise gives you repeatable steps to validate your transaction-sending code before moving to a live network.

keyIdea.title: Lab outcome
keyIdea.text: Deploy, send increment and decrement transactions, capture hashes and receipts, and handle a deliberate revert.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Counter Exercise
sendTx.js (structure)
// Setup provider and ABIs
// Web3.js: connect, get accounts, call increment().send({ from, gas })
// Ethers.js: create Wallet with private key, contract with signer, call increment() then await tx.wait()
// After each receipt: console.log receipt and contract.count()
Expected outputs
  • Transaction hashes printed for each send.
  • Receipt objects with gasUsed and blockNumber after wait.
  • Updated count printed after successful transactions.
  • Caught revert and error message when decrement fails at zero.
Safety reminder
Use Ganache accounts only for local testing; never expose private keys in logs or source control.

screens.title: Web3.js vs Ethers.js: Transaction Patterns
screens.subtitle: How each library handles sending, signing, and receipts

narration.text: Both Web3. js and Ethers. js let you interact with contracts, but they emphasize slightly different patterns for transactions. Web3. js gives you a send method on contract methods that accepts an options object and returns a Promise that resolves to a receipt once mined. This means the call itself produces the mined receipt when awaited. Ethers. js, by contrast, separates submission from confirmation: calling a contract method through a signer returns a transaction response immediately with a hash, and you then call wait on that response to receive the receipt. In practice, both approaches produce the same on-chain result; the difference affects UI design. With Ethers you can show the hash instantly and update progress while waiting for wait to resolve. With Web3. js you await the Promise for the mined receipt directly. A misconception is that one library is inherently faster — inclusion speed is governed by gas settings and the network, not the client library. Choose the pattern that fits your UI flow and be consistent about how you display pending versus confirmed states. Both libraries require the same safety checks: estimate gas, check balances, avoid hardcoding private keys, and handle reverts gracefully.

keyIdea.title: Practical contrast
keyIdea.text: Web3 returns the mined receipt from .send(); Ethers returns an immediate tx response and requires tx.wait() for the receipt.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Web3 vs Ethers
Web3.js
  • .send() with options returns a Promise resolving to the mined receipt.
  • Good for straightforward flows where you await finality in one step.
  • Example: myContract.methods.updateMessage(msg).send({ from, gas })
Ethers.js
  • Contract calls with a Signer return a tx response. Call tx.wait() to receive the receipt.
  • Enables immediate UX with tx.hash before confirmation.
  • Example: const tx = await contract.updateMessage(msg); await tx.wait();
Key Takeaway

Both libraries are valid choices; pick the UX pattern you prefer and enforce the same safety checks in either case.

screens.title: Private Keys and Safe Signing Practices
screens.subtitle: Never hardcode keys; prefer injected providers for production

narration.text: Security is critical when dealing with transactions: a leaked private key allows anyone to sign transactions and drain funds. For local testing on Ganache it is acceptable to use a private key in a script, but never commit keys to source control or embed them in production code. The recommended production pattern is to use an injected provider like a browser wallet which supplies a Signer without exposing the private key to your application code. Another safe practice is to minimize on-chain value exposure during testing and to rotate keys if they are ever printed or logged. A practical misconception to correct: storing keys in environment variables is slightly safer than in code, but still risky if the environment or CI logs are compromised. Also avoid broadcasting raw private keys to third-party services. For DApp UX, explain to users how transactions are signed and prompt them for confirmations in the wallet UI. This reduces surprise and builds trust. In short: use injected signers, avoid hardcoding, and keep private material strictly out of your app bundle. Private Keys and Safe Signing Practices means never hardcode private keys in production; use injected providers or wallet-based signers to keep keys client-side and user-controlled.. In practical terms, never hardcode keys; prefer injected providers for production. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Security rule
keyIdea.text: Never hardcode private keys in production; use injected providers or wallet-based signers to keep keys client-side and user-controlled.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Private Key Safety
Safe signing practices
  • Use injected providers (browser wallets) so users sign locally without exposing keys to your app.
  • For local scripts, keep private keys out of source control and never log them.
  • If a key is exposed, rotate accounts and invalidate compromised credentials immediately.
  • Explain signing to users so they can recognize legitimate wallet prompts and avoid phishing attacks.
Warning

Never hardcode a private key in production. The example in this chapter uses Ganache keys only for local development.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Key Concepts
Transaction Receipt
Contains gas used, block number, and logs you can use to update the application state.
Reverts & Costs
A revert stops state change but still consumes gas; handle reverts in catch blocks and inform the user.
Signer & Security
Use a wallet-provided signer in production. Never hardcode private keys or expose them in the client or logs.
Final takeaway
Combine reliable gas estimation, clear UX for pending/confirmed states, and robust error handling to build dependable transaction flows in your DApps.

ai_generation_note:
Create a 15-minute live coding video. Start with a quick review of the `MyMutableContract.sol` and `Counter.sol` contracts. Demonstrate deploying `Counter.sol` to Ganache. Then, in VS Code, live code the `sendTx.js` script. Show the initial `count`, then execute the `increment()` transaction using both Web3.js and Ethers.js, highlighting the `send()` and `tx.wait()` calls. Display the transaction hashes and the updated `count` after each operation. Crucially, demonstrate the `decrement()` function, first successfully, then intentionally trigger the `require(count > 0)` revert, showing how the `try...catch` block captures the error and logs it. Include visual overlays explaining gas parameters and a warning about private key usage in production. End with a 3-question interactive quiz on gas concepts and transaction lifecycle.
